transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Ortega (Redwood Solutions), Amara Singh (CTO, Vela Labs), Diego Morales (Head of Security), Hannah Park (Cloud Infra), Owen Li (Platform Eng)

Summary: short technical deep-dive on private deployment security guardrails — network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling patterns, KMS/encryption integration, audit logging, and SOC2/ISO evidence needs. Customer concerned about data residency, auditability, and runbook ops for key compromise.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro from our side, i'm maya with redwood, this is ravi our solutions engineer and lina on solutions as well.
[00:23] Amara Singh: thanks maya, appreciate it. we'll do intros quick — i'm amara, cto, diego is our head of security, hannah runs our cloud infra, owen is platform. busy week for us so we'll dive in.
[00:36] Ravi Patel: cool, high level agenda: private deployment topology, VPC peering vs private link, ingress patterns, egress proxy and firewall rules, KMS integration and key rotation, audit logs and SOC2 artifacts. we'll try to keep this hands on and then capture action items.
[01:15] Diego Morales: big focus for us is auditability and key custody. we need to be able to show auditors that keys are rotated, that access is RBAC controlled and that logs are tamper-evident. also data must remain in EU region for certain customers.
[01:42] Ravi Patel: understood. on key custody we commonly integrate with customer KMS (cloud KMS / HSM) and provide a key-handover handshake for envelopes so the private deploy doesn't store plaintext keys. little bit of nuance on rotate flows but we can show an example.
[02:10] Hannah Park: how does your runtime handle access to KV cache and model weights? do those sit on the local nodes or are they pulled from S3/backing store? if they live on NVMe we need disk encryption and node isolation policies.
[02:33] Ravi Patel: good question. model weights are pulled during boot from your object store and cached on node local NVMe, we recommend using encrypted volumes (LUKS/TDE depending on distro) and mount options. the runtime exposes a lockfile for in-flight KV cache but we can mount that on ephemeral storage and ensure it's wiped on node termination.
[03:01] Amara Singh: are there documented steps for airgap installs? some of our regulated pods need limited egress to only approved repos.
[03:18] Lina Ortega: yes, we have an airgapped install playbook; it's a bit different than the public private deploy — we'll send the checklist. it includes allowed registries, a hashed artifact manifest and offline package verification.
[03:45] Owen Li: on the network side we're debating between VPC peering and a PrivateLink style proxy. any tradeoffs?
[03:58] Ravi Patel: VPC peering is simpler but cross-tenant route tables can get messy; PrivateLink (or equivalent mTLS ingress proxy) provides tighter control and avoids full route table exposure. for egress control we recommend funneling outbound through an approved NAT + egress proxy with allowlists.
[04:30] Diego Morales: acceptable, but we also need deep packet inspection on egress for suspicious exfil patterns. can the egress proxy support custom inspection hooks?
[04:45] Ravi Patel: the typical pattern is egress goes to your perimeter firewall cluster — we forward via an internal proxy that can integrate with your DLP or IDS. Redwood's runtime emits structured request logs and headers so you can correlate requests upstream. note — sometimes the agent name in logs is transcribed as 'redwood node' or 'red node' in early logs so auditors need mapping.
[05:20] Amara Singh: about RBAC and SSO — can we map our existing groups from Okta into role assignments?
[05:34] Maya Chen: yes, we support SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning, you can map Okta groups to Redwood roles. for private deploys the control plane can be self-hosted (we call that private control plane) and you can keep auth inside your VPC.
[06:05] Hannah Park: what granularity of audit logs do you expose? we need user-level actions, token usage, model version deployments, and admin policy changes.
[06:22] Ravi Patel: logs include API-level events (create/invoke/model version), token issuance/rotation, and node lifecycle events. retention is configurable — we ship to your SIEM via syslog/HTTPS. small caveat: early versions had incomplete key rotate events labeled as 'tok rotate' in logs, which is a known mapping issue; we've fixed that in 2026.12 release but auditors sometimes see older labels.
[06:55] Diego Morales: ok. about data residency — some datasets must never leave eu-west-1, if we run inference across regions for burst capacity, how is that handled?
[07:12] Ravi Patel: you can pin workloads to region-specific pools. Smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants in other regions but we can disable cross-region fallback for constrained tenants. we'll show you policy examples in the diagram.
[07:40] Amara Singh: let's walk the network diagram.
[07:50] Ravi Patel: (screen share described) imagine three subnet groups: management/control, runtime/worker, and shared services. control plane components (scheduler, config) sit in management subnets with restricted inbound. worker nodes run in private subnets with no public IPs. ingress for customer traffic is through an internal ALB + mTLS gateway — we prefer a mutual TLS fronting layer so we can authenticate both sides.
[08:30] Owen Li: for mTLS do you expect us to manage certs or can Redwood manage cert rotation?
[08:42] Ravi Patel: you can do either. common pattern: customer-managed CA issued certs for mTLS and we integrate with your cert manager (vault/cert-manager). Redwood can also operate cert rotation but customers in regulated sectors often insist on customer control.
[09:10] Maya Chen: just calling out SOC 2 scoping — auditors will want to see RBAC matrix, evidence of key rotation, and log retention policy. we typically provide a packaged evidence bundle for private deployments referencing your control plane logs.
[09:33] Diego Morales: what about HSM integration? we use vendor Y HSM for production keys.
[09:43] Ravi Patel: HSM integrations are supported — we do a KMIP/PKCS#11 bridge or cloud KMS API depending on vendor. we recommend using envelope encryption: model keys are wrapped by HSM-managed keys, application never sees plaintext. rotation: perform rewrap flows and record a rewrap event in audit logs.
[10:10] Hannah Park: walk me through a key compromise scenario and recovery steps.
[10:20] Ravi Patel: typical playbook: detect via alert -> revoke KMS key and replace with rotated key -> rewrap model keys -> restart runtime nodes to ensure caches are evicted -> run integrity check. we can provide a runbook with exact CLI steps.
[10:45] Amara Singh: cache eviction sounds disruptive. is there a way to do live rekey without full restarts?
[10:55] Ravi Patel: for some runtime components yes, we support in-place KV cache invalidation and lazy rewrap of new tokens, but full rewrap of model weights often requires node bounce to guarantee no plaintext remains on disk. we document graceful drain procedures to minimize request impact.
[11:25] Owen Li: what network policies should we apply for inter-pod communication? we're Kubernetes-based.
[11:36] Ravi Patel: CNI network policies to restrict kube-system <-> runtime namespaces, deny default allow rules. We recommend egress deny-by-default with explicit allowlists for object storage, private control plane endpoints, and your SIEM. Also use PodSecurityPolicies or OPA Gatekeeper for admission control.
[12:00] Hannah Park: do you have recommendations for firewall rules — for example, minimal port set we should open?
[12:08] Lina Ortega: yes, we'll send a prescriptive list but short version: control plane TLS ports (443/8443) from management bastion IPs only, worker nodes only need outbound to object storage and KMS endpoints on port 443, mTLS ingress ports on 8443 for mutual TLS, and node-to-node gRPC on 8070 (example) should be internal-only.
[12:40] Diego Morales: how do we prove immutability of logs to auditors? do you support pushing to WORM storage or S3 object lock?
[12:53] Ravi Patel: we can forward logs to your WORM-compliant bucket with object lock enabled, and we support write-once retention windows. additionally you can stream to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) with signed delivery and retention controls.
[13:20] Amara Singh: any gotchas with offline backups for model artifacts for compliance? we need hashed archives and chain of custody.
[13:33] Lina Ortega: the airgap playbook covers generating SHA256 manifests, timestamped signatures, and we advise storing manifests in a separate immutable archive with access controls. auditors like signatures from your private key.
[14:00] Maya Chen: shifting to runtime-level metrics — what traces do you surface for request provenance so we can trace back a customer request to a token and node id?
[14:12] Ravi Patel: each request gets a unique request id, token id is redacted in logs but traceable via token issuance events in the control plane. we map node id, pod name, and if enabled the KV cache hit ratio. note: older log schema used 'session' instead of 'request id' — if you're pulling historic logs we can translate.
[14:45] Diego Morales: on RBAC, can we have time-bound admin roles for emergency access?
[14:55] Maya Chen: yes, you can use ephemeral admin roles via your IdP with SSO + short TTL sessions; we recommend just-in-time access with approval workflow.
[15:20] Hannah Park: network egress — you mentioned funneling through a proxy; do you support an internal TLS tunnel to our egress cluster?
[15:33] Ravi Patel: yes, runtime can route outbound through a TLS tunnel or internal proxy with mTLS. that proxy can then perform token-level inspection and route to external destinations.
[16:05] Owen Li: for outbound allowlists do you have an allowlist template for object store, KMS and external registries?
[16:18] Lina Ortega: yes, we'll attach a template. basics: S3 endpoints, KMS endpoints (region-specific), registry FQDNs plus fingerprinted cert pins for registries in airgap.
[16:45] Amara Singh: compliance question — SOC2 auditors ask for separation of duties. how do you show that Redwood operations and our ops don't overlap?
[16:58] Maya Chen: for private control plane, we can show RBAC separation and that Redwood's support access is subject to explicit SSO-based approvals and SAML group assignments; also export access logs showing which user performed privileged actions.
[17:30] Diego Morales: can we enforce network microsegmentation between different customers on same physical cluster?
[17:44] Ravi Patel: multi-tenancy on same cluster is doable with strict namespace isolation, CNI policies, and encryption at rest; however, for strong isolation we recommend dedicated capacity (reserved pools) per tenant. Redwood Dedicated offers per-tenant GPU pools, otherwise use hard tenancy via node taints + topology spread.
[18:10] Hannah Park: about firewalling, do you have recommendations for stateful vs stateless firewalls, and any vendor-specific notes (we use Palo Alto Panorama)?
[18:22] Ravi Patel: stateful firewalls are preferred for egress inspection. for Palo Alto you can push policies via Panorama and we publish an example rule set. For high-throughput, avoid throughput-heavy DPI on latency-sensitive paths — move DPI to a mirrored flow or sample-based inspection.
[18:54] Amara Singh: what logging level increases would affect performance? if we enable debug for request tracing, will that hurt latency?
[19:07] Ravi Patel: heavy synchronous logging can add tail latency. recommended pattern: quick structured event emission asynchronously to a local buffer then ship. synchronous full-request dumps only during incident windows.
[19:40] Owen Li: any suggestions for key rotation windows? auditors often expect rotation cadence.
[19:52] Diego Morales: we target 90 days but can accept 365 for wrapped keys if HSM provided.
[20:01] Ravi Patel: common: rotate wrapping keys (HSM) annually and rewrap material keys quarterly; exact cadence should be risk-based. we can show baseline policy.
[20:30] Amara Singh: can you show a sample evidence bundle for SOC2?
[20:40] Maya Chen: yes we'll include RBAC matrix, sample audit log extracts, KMS integration diagram, and our control mappings to SOC2/ISO clauses.
[21:05] Hannah Park: what about retention costs for logs — do you have guidance for managing cost vs retention?
[21:18] Lina Ortega: set tiered retention: immediate hot retention in SIEM for 90 days, then move to cold storage (compressed) for longer windows; export only indexes required for audit. we can provide a cost estimate template.
[21:45] Diego Morales: question about ingress authentication — can we do per-customer mTLS certs + JWT tokens?
[21:55] Ravi Patel: yes, mTLS for transport and JWT for per-request identity works well. JWTs can be short lived and issued by your IdP; Redwood validates tokens at the gateway.
[22:20] Amara Singh: any known issues with certain distros or kernel versions? we've had trouble with hugepage behavior affecting inference.
[22:34] Ravi Patel: we document supported kernels; hugepages can affect memory accounting — we recommend swappiness tuning and preallocating hugepages on the platform nodes. we'll attach our compatibility matrix.
[23:00] Maya Chen: quick pause — are there specific audit questions you want us to answer in the artifact bundle?
[23:10] Diego Morales: yes: need a narrative for key custody, list of endpoints we access, list of privileged Redwood users and their access method, proof of log shipping.
[23:30] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include a narrative and export config snippets.
[24:00] Ravi Patel: moving to an example egress playbook — step 1: deny-by-default on egress; step 2: create allowlists for object store/KMS/registry; step 3: route through egress proxy with TLS termination and DLP hooks; step 4: mirror suspicious flows to IDS.
[24:35] Owen Li: for allowlist maintenance, do you support FQDN-based or CIDR-based rules?
[24:45] Lina Ortega: both, but FQDN with DNS-resolve is easier operationally; for strict compliance CIDR allowlists are preferred. in airgap envs we recommend pinned certs and static IP mapping.
[25:10] Amara Singh: are there metrics you recommend exposing for SRE to measure security posture?
[25:20] Ravi Patel: token issuance rates, failed auth attempts, key rotate events, cache purge counts, inbound mTLS failure rates, and egress deny hits.
[25:50] Hannah Park: what about incident response? can we get a sample playbook for suspected exfil?
[26:02] Lina Ortega: yes — detect, isolate affected nodes by cordon/taint, revoke keys, rotate wrappers, and preserve forensic logs to a WORM bucket. we'll attach a template.
[26:35] Diego Morales: does Redwood provide runbook automation (playbooks) or is it manual ops?
[26:45] Ravi Patel: we have integrations with your orchestration (Argo/Ansible) to automate node drain and redeploy, but many customers prefer to operate playbooks through their own runbook automation.
[27:10] Amara Singh: about model artifacts, can we encrypt them with our key before they hit object store?
[27:22] Ravi Patel: yes, client-side encryption with your key is supported; Redwood will accept wrapped artifacts and then perform envelope decryption at runtime using keys from your KMS.
[27:50] Owen Li: any example of how to map our firewall rules to the runtime?
[28:00] Ravi Patel: we'll provide an example JSON manifest mapping ports and FQDNs to security group rules; for Palo Alto we provided a sample rule set in a previous customer repo.
[28:30] Maya Chen: quick check on timelines — you mentioned pilot in May, is that still target?
[28:40] Amara Singh: yes week of may 3rd looks good but need to confirm internal sign-offs.
[29:00] Diego Morales: procurement also asked about indemnity and data breach SLA. who owns what?
[29:12] Maya Chen: contract can include a responsibility matrix; for private deployments customers generally retain responsibility for network controls and data at rest, Redwood covers runtime code and patching; we'll loop in legal for exact language.
[29:45] Hannah Park: on patching windows, how do you handle CVE responses for runtime?
[29:55] Ravi Patel: we publish CVE advisories and provide hotfix images; in private deploys you apply patches and we support the rollout plan; for critical CVEs we push a coordinated emergency patch with recommended mitigation steps.
[30:20] Owen Li: question on observability retention — can we filter PII from logs before shipping?
[30:33] Ravi Patel: yes, we have PII scrubbers and configurable redaction rules at the gateway. default sanitization removes likely PII but you should provide allowlist/denylist rules.
[31:00] Amara Singh: how do we demonstrate separation of dev/test and prod to auditors?
[31:12] Maya Chen: show separate VPCs/subscriptions, distinct KMS keys, separate log buckets and CI/CD pipelines with role gating. we'll prepare a checklist.
[31:40] Diego Morales: for disaster recovery, if a region fails can we restore into another region without violating data residency?
[31:52] Ravi Patel: restore-to-other-region is possible but must be gated by policy; we recommend runbook steps to rehydrate only permitted datasets and to notify legal and data owners. for strict residency we advise manual approval before cross-region restore.
[32:20] Hannah Park: any performance impacts from encryption at rest + KMS calls on inference latency?
[32:33] Ravi Patel: envelope encryption means only initial unwrap touches KMS; after that keys are cached locally in memory. KMS latency on unwrap is a one-time startup cost per node, not per request. impact on steady-state inference is negligible.
[33:00] Maya Chen: let's cover audit log examples you'll want: token issuance, key rotate, node boot with image digest, admin policy change, and export of RBAC mapping.
[33:18] Diego Morales: good. can you provide log snippets that won't leak customer data?
[33:30] Lina Ortega: yes, sanitized log extracts with redacted tokens and pseudonymized ids.
[34:00] Owen Li: any tips on minimizing blast radius for misconfigured ingress rules?
[34:12] Ravi Patel: implement network policy enforcement and use egress/ingress canaries. also apply mutating admission webhooks to deny deployments with hostNetwork or hostPath.
[34:40] Amara Singh: what about runtime telemetry — does it include model provenance? we need which model version answered which request.
[34:53] Ravi Patel: yes request logs include model id, model version, and config flags. auditors like to see immutable model manifests in artifact store with checksums.
[35:20] Hannah Park: are there known issues integrating with our SIEM (we use Splunk Cloud) for high-volume logs?
[35:34] Lina Ortega: we have a Splunk HEC forwarder pattern and recommend batching to avoid rate limits; we can provide a template with retry/backoff.
[36:00] Maya Chen: recent question — do you need agent-level secrets beyond KMS?
[36:12] Ravi Patel: some connectors need service principals for object store; those should be short-lived or scoped least-privilege and rotated regularly. we avoid storing long-lived plaintext creds.
[36:40] Diego Morales: let's set the concrete next steps and owners.
[36:50] Maya Chen: recap: we'll send network diagram, firewall rule template, SOC2 artifact bundle and an airgap checklist. ravi will prepare the KMS runbook and rotate playbook. hannah will share ingress IPs and expected traffic pattern.
[37:10] Amara Singh: sounds good.
[37:25] Owen Li: small operational ask — can we get a sample terraform module for security groups?
[37:34] Lina Ortega: yes, we'll attach a sample terraform module that maps to the allowlist template.
[37:50] Hannah Park: on the pilot benchmarks, what metrics will you run?
[37:58] Ravi Patel: latency p95/p99, token cost, throughput per GPU, and cold-start time with encrypted volumes. also measurement of log shipping latencies.
[38:20] Diego Morales: one more question — do you support customer-managed telemetry endpoints for tracing?
[38:31] Ravi Patel: yes, you can configure OpenTelemetry exporters to your trace backend.
[38:55] Amara Singh: ok any final gotchas?
[39:05] Ravi Patel: two quick notes: 1) ensure node boot image digests are pinned in your image registry to satisfy audit checks; 2) double-check your retention law for logs in the region especially if EU customers have conflicting requests.
[39:30] Maya Chen: that wraps the technical portion, we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the pilot kickoff.
[39:45] Amara Singh: thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity.
[40:00] (small side conversation / cross talk)
[41:10] Maya Chen: final quick action items captured in chat. we'll send a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff week of 2027-05-03.
[41:30] Diego Morales: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
